lead: A level is a telescope that can be made to look along a horizontal line, mounted so that it can turn in a horizontal circle. Every reading in levelling assumes that the line of sight is truly horizontal when the bubble is centred. Two kinds of adjustment make that true. Temporary adjustments are done at every set-up: setting up, levelling up and removing parallax. Permanent adjustments are done only when a test shows the instrument's own lines are out of their proper relation; the most important is the two-peg test for the line of collimation.
prereq: You need: backsight, foresight, height of instrument and reduced level from Levelling terms: datum, benchmark, reduced level.

sections.h3: Types of level and their parts

items: Dumpy level: telescope fixed rigidly to the vertical spindle, bubble tube on top; levelled with three foot screws.
Tilting level: a tilting screw tilts the telescope slightly, so the main bubble is centred quickly for each sight.
Automatic level: a hanging prism compensator keeps the line of sight horizontal once a circular bubble is centred; the common site instrument today.
Digital level: an automatic level that reads a bar-coded staff and stores the readings. Older texts also describe the wye (Y) level.

blocks.text: The main parts of a dumpy level are the telescope (objective lens, eyepiece, and the diaphragm carrying the cross-hairs), the focusing screw, the bubble tube (a curved vial whose axis is horizontal when the bubble is central), the levelling head with three foot screws, and the tripod. The levelling staff is usually a 4 m folding or telescopic staff graduated every 5 mm, read to the millimetre.

Three lines matter. The vertical axis is the axis the instrument turns about. The axis of the bubble tube is the tangent to the vial's curve at its centre. The line of collimation joins the intersection of the cross-hairs to the optical centre of the objective. For a correct dumpy level: (1) the bubble axis is perpendicular to the vertical axis, (2) the line of collimation is parallel to the bubble axis, and (3) the horizontal cross-hair lies in a plane perpendicular to the vertical axis.

items: Setting up. Plant the tripod firmly and bring the head roughly level by moving the legs.

Levelling up. With the telescope parallel to two foot screws, turn them together (thumbs both inward or both outward) until the bubble is central; the bubble follows the left thumb. Turn through 90° over the third screw and centre the bubble with it alone. Repeat until the bubble stays central in every direction.
Focusing the eyepiece on the cross-hairs against a bright background.
Focusing the objective on the staff with the focusing screw.
Removing parallax. If the cross-hair seems to move on the staff when the eye moves, the image is not in the plane of the cross-hairs; refocus until it does not.

sections.h3: Permanent adjustments and the two-peg test

blocks.text: Permanent adjustments correct the instrument itself, in this order:

items: Bubble tube adjustment (bubble axis perpendicular to the vertical axis). Level up carefully, then turn the telescope through 180°. If the bubble moves off centre, bring it halfway back with the capstan screws at one end of the bubble tube and the other half with the foot screws. Repeat until the bubble stays central in all directions.

Cross-hair ring adjustment (horizontal hair perpendicular to the vertical axis). A point sighted at one end of the horizontal hair must stay on it as the telescope turns; if not, rotate the diaphragm ring.

Collimation adjustment (line of collimation parallel to the bubble axis), by the two-peg test. If the line of sight tilts by α, a reading at distance D is wrong by D tan α; equal sights cancel this, so the test uses unequal sights.

blocks.text: The two-peg test uses two pegs A and B about 100 m apart:

items: Set up exactly midway at C and read both staffs. The two readings carry equal error, so their difference is the true difference of level.
Move the level to a point D on the line BA produced, a short distance beyond A, and read both staffs again.
Let e be the error per metre of sight. Then (reading on B − DB·e) − (reading on A − DA·e) = true difference. Solve for e.

Compute the correct reading on B, (reading on B) − DB·e. With the level still at D, move the horizontal cross-hair with the diaphragm screws (dumpy level), or bring the line of sight to the correct reading with the tilting screw and then re-centre the bubble with its capstan screws (tilting level). On an automatic level the reticule is adjusted.

blocks.text: e = [(b₂ − a₂) − (b₁ − a₁)] ÷ (DB − DA);   α = tan⁻¹ e
blocks.where: a₁, b₁ are the readings on A and B from the midpoint; a₂, b₂ the readings from D; DA, DB the distances from D to A and B in metres. A positive e means the line of sight points upward (readings too large).

blocks.text: The sensitivity of a bubble tube is the angle the line of sight tilts when the bubble moves one division. Read a staff at distance D, move the bubble n divisions with a foot screw and read again; if the reading changes by s, the sensitivity is α = s ÷ (nD) radians, or 206 265 × s ÷ (nD) seconds.

examples.question: Two pegs A and B are 100 m apart. With the level midway, the readings are 1.625 m on A and 2.115 m on B. The level is then set up at D, 10 m from A on the line BA produced (so DB = 110 m), and the readings are 1.435 m on A and 1.943 m on B. (a) Find the true difference of level between A and B. (b) Is the line of collimation inclined upward or downward, and by what angle? (c) What should the staff on B read when the instrument at D is in adjustment? (d) Check your answer.
steps: (a) From the midpoint the errors cancel: true difference = b₁ − a₁ = 2.115 − 1.625 = 0.490 m. B reads more, so B is 0.490 m lower than A.
(b) Apparent difference from D = b₂ − a₂ = 1.943 − 1.435 = 0.508 m.
The extra 0.508 − 0.490 = 0.018 m builds up over the extra sight length DB − DA = 110 − 10 = 100 m, so e = 0.018 ÷ 100 = 0.00018 m per metre.
e is positive, so the far reading is too large: the line of sight is inclined upward. α = tan⁻¹(0.00018) = 0.00018 rad × 206 265 = 37″ (about 37 seconds).
(d) Check: 1.923 − 1.433 = 0.490 m, the true difference. Adjust until B reads 1.923 m with the bubble central.
examples.answer: True difference 0.490 m (B lower). The line of collimation is inclined upward by about 37″ (0.018 m in 100 m). With the level at D, the staff on B should read 1.923 m.

traps: Taking the difference from the second set-up as the true one. Only the midpoint readings give the true difference, because equal sights cancel the collimation error.
Correcting the whole bubble error with the capstan screws. In the bubble tube adjustment, half the error is the instrument's (capstan screws) and half is the levelling (foot screws).
Doing the two-peg test with parallax or a moving bubble. Temporary adjustments come first, or a correct instrument gets “adjusted” wrongly.
Naming the wrong order. Permanent adjustments of a dumpy level: bubble tube first, then the cross-hair ring, then the line of collimation.

quiz.q: List the temporary adjustments of a level in order.
quiz.a: Setting up (with rough levelling by the legs), levelling up with the foot screws, focusing the eyepiece, focusing the objective and removing parallax.

quiz.q: What is parallax, and how is it removed?
quiz.a: Apparent movement of the cross-hair against the staff when the eye moves, because the image is not in the plane of the cross-hairs. Focus the eyepiece on the cross-hairs, then refocus the objective until the movement disappears.

quiz.q: In a two-peg test, the midpoint readings are 1.250 m on A and 1.880 m on B (pegs 80 m apart). From a point 8 m beyond A (88 m from B), the readings are 1.142 m on A and 1.756 m on B. Find the collimation error per metre and its direction.
quiz.a: True difference = 0.630 m; apparent = 0.614 m. e = (0.614 − 0.630) ÷ 80 = −0.0002 m per metre: the line of sight is inclined downward (readings too small) by about 41″.

quiz.q: A bubble tube has a sensitivity of 20″ per division. If the bubble is 2 divisions off centre, what is the error in a reading at 60 m?
A level with a collimation error is used with every backsight 40 m and every foresight 40 m. Will the RLs be wrong? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Each reading is too large (or too small) by the same 40e, and RL = RL + BS − FS uses the difference, so the error cancels. That is why sights are balanced in practice; intermediate sights at other distances are still affected.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern automatic levels use magnetically or air-damped compensators that settle within a second, and digital levels compute collimation error themselves from a built-in two-peg routine and correct every reading. Laser levels and rotating lasers now set out floor and formation levels directly, and machine-control systems on graders read a laser plane. Search for compensator accuracy, digital level collimation test and rotating laser level.

figure.caption: The two-peg test of the worked example. From the midpoint C both readings carry the same error, so they give the true difference of 0.490 m. From D the far sight is 100 m longer, so its extra 0.018 m is the collimation error: the staff on B should read 1.923 m.
